caption:
Why was Abu Simbel moved?

Because the Aswan High Dam would have raised the water up to 60 metres over it, and wet sandstone loses its strength.

Ramesses II had two temples cut into the cliff from about 1264 BC; the work took roughly twenty years. Then sand buried the Great Temple — by the 6th century BC up to the statues' knees. Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found it in 1813 with one head and part of a chest above the drift. Giovanni Belzoni's party dug for 22 days and got inside on 1 August 1817; Giovanni Finati, the slenderest of them, crept through first.

Rescue schemes included leaving the temples underwater behind a dam of clear filtered water, viewed from glass galleries, and floating them up on concrete barges. The plan chosen was to saw the temples into blocks and rebuild them uphill, estimated at $36 million — half the cost of the rest. It came to 1,036 blocks, the smallest seven tons. Crowns were cut off because the heads exceeded the 30-ton lifting limit, and the faces were sawn away from behind the ears.

The Great Temple was rebuilt 208 m inland and 65 m higher, with a permitted deviation of 5 mm, so the sun would still reach the sanctuary on 22 February and 22 October. Ptah, god of the realm of the dead, stays unlit.

Still open: the dates. They are said to be the king's birthday and coronation day, with no direct evidence. Earth's axial precession means the original date was different anyway — and because the temple was moved, the alignment may not be as precise as it once was.

Images: Maxime Du Camp, 1850; Francis Frith, 1857; Per-Olow Anderson, 1967; modern views by Olaf Tausch, Gary Todd and Than217.
